title: Where Does the Solar System End?

pages.text: A football sails over the school wall and out of sight. Where does the field really end? Astronomers ask the same question about the Solar System. Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. It orbits at about 30 astronomical units. One astronomical unit, or AU, is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres. But the Solar System does not stop at Neptune. Beyond it lies the Kuiper Belt (say KY-per), a wide ring of icy objects stretching from about 30 to 50 AU. These objects are leftovers from the time the planets formed, 4.6 billion years ago. Pluto is the best known of them. In 2015, the New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto and sent back the first close-up pictures of its mountains of ice.

pages.text: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is round, but it shares its orbit with many other objects. Five are officially recognised. Ceres lies in the asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter. The other four, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris, lie beyond Neptune. Eris surprised astronomers when it was found in 2005. It is slightly smaller than Pluto but has about a quarter more mass. Its orbit is a long, stretched oval. It swings from 38 AU out to 98 AU and takes about 560 years to go round once. Astronomers expect to confirm more dwarf planets as telescopes improve.

pages.text: The Sun does not only give out light. It also blows out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind. This wind rushes past all the planets and pushes back the thin gas that drifts between the stars. The result is a giant bubble around the Solar System, called the heliosphere. The name comes from helios, the Greek word for Sun. The outer edge of the bubble is the heliopause. It lies about 120 AU from the Sun, four times as far as Neptune. Inside it, the Sun’s wind is in charge. Outside it is interstellar space: the space between the stars.

pages.text: Only two spacecraft have ever crossed the heliopause. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 were launched in 1977 to study the giant planets. They never stopped. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in August 2012. Voyager 2 followed in November 2018. Both still send faint radio signals home. NASA calculated that on 18 November 2026 Voyager 1 would be one light-day from Earth. That is about 25.9 billion kilometres, or 173 AU. A radio signal travels at the speed of light, yet it needs a full day to reach the spacecraft. Voyager 1 is the most distant object people have ever made.

pages.text: Far beyond the heliopause, astronomers think there is a vast shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole Solar System. It is called the Oort Cloud, after the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort, who predicted it in 1950. Nobody has seen it directly. Its objects are too small, too dark, and too far away. The evidence comes from comets. Some comets fall towards the Sun from enormous distances and from every direction, as if from a giant shell. The Oort Cloud may begin about 1,000 AU from the Sun and stretch to 100,000 AU. Voyager 1 covers about 3.5 AU a year. Even so, it will need more than 200 years to reach the inner edge.

pages.text: The answer depends on what you mean by edge. If you mean the last planet, the Solar System ends at Neptune, 30 AU out. If you mean the reach of the solar wind, it ends at the heliopause, about 120 AU out. If you mean the reach of the Sun’s gravity, it ends at the outer Oort Cloud, perhaps 100,000 AU away. That is more than a third of the way to the nearest star. And the map is not finished. Some astronomers suspect that an undiscovered planet orbits far beyond Neptune. A powerful new telescope in Chile, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, began scanning the southern sky in 2025. It may settle the question.

activities.question: What is the Kuiper Belt?
options: A belt of rocky asteroids between Mars and Jupiter
A wide ring of icy objects beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 AU

activities.question: What creates the heliosphere?
options: The solar wind pushing back the thin gas between the stars

activities.question: Nobody has seen the Oort Cloud. Why do astronomers think it exists?
options: Some comets arrive from enormous distances and from every direction
It can be seen without a telescope on dark nights

activities.question: Apply it: A spacecraft is 150 AU from the Sun. Which statement is true?
options: It is still inside the Kuiper Belt
It has passed the nearest star
It has left the heliosphere but has not reached the Oort Cloud

activities.prompt: Arrange from nearest the Sun to farthest.

activities.definition: The giant bubble around the Solar System made by the solar wind.
distractors: The hot surface of the Sun
The layer of air around Earth

glossary.definition: The Kuiper Belt: a wide ring of icy objects beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 AU.
The bubble around the Solar System created by the solar wind.
The outer edge of the heliosphere, about 120 AU from the Sun.
Interstellar space: the space between the stars, outside the heliosphere.
The Oort Cloud: a predicted shell of icy bodies far beyond the planets; the source of many comets.
